children: By Rolfe Winkler and Robbie Whelan
Cloud-computing company CoreWeave said that it met Wall Street's expectations for its third-quarter results, tamping down fears about its business, at least for the moment.

The so-called neocloud company — which buys advanced AI chips known as graphics processing units from Nvidia, installs them in data centers and leases them to companies such as Microsoft and OpenAI — reported revenue of $3.7 billion for the quarter that ended in September. And it said its backlog of business hit $133 billion. Analysts polled by S&P Global had expected quarterly revenue of $3.6 billion and a backlog of $131 billion.
The company's shares rose 6% in after-hours trading after closing Tuesday at $48.73.

CoreWeave's shares have more than halved since it last reported results in August. The free fall was sparked, in part, by the company's rising borrowing costs. Its unsecured debt now sports yields around 15%, which is prohibitively expensive if the company were forced to raise such debt to finance more construction.
CoreWeave's Chief Executive, Michael Intrator, sought to tamp down concerns about the company's financing costs.

"Our growth is supported by multiple sources of funding, including financing backed by customer contracts, operating cash flow, and approximately $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits expected in the next three months alone," he said. "That financial flexibility positions us to keep delivering the infrastructure and software customers need to build, run, and scale AI."
